hints: Remember Le Chatelier's principle handles temperature and pressure separately, so check what each change favours for the forward reaction.
Increasing temperature moves equilibrium in the endothermic direction, so for a rightward shift the forward $\Delta H$ must be positive.
Decreasing pressure moves equilibrium toward the side with more moles of gas, so count gas moles on left and right to find where the right side is larger.
walkthrough:
**Use temperature to find the sign of ΔH**

Increasing temperature adds heat. Equilibrium shifts to use up that heat, which is the endothermic direction.

We want a shift to the right, so the forward reaction must be endothermic with $\Delta H > 0$.

**Shortlist using ΔH values**

Look at the given data:
$$\text{A: } \Delta H = +40 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \text{ (forward endothermic)}$$
$$\text{B: } \Delta H = +58 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \text{ (forward endothermic)}$$
$$\text{C: } \Delta H = -197 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \text{ (forward exothermic)}$$
$$\text{D: } \Delta H = -10 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \text{ (forward exothermic)}$$
Only A and B shift right when heated. C and D would shift left.

**Use pressure to compare gas moles**

Decreasing pressure favours the side with more moles of gas, because more particles create more pressure.

Count gas moles left vs right:
$$\text{A: 2 } \rightleftharpoons \text{ 2, no change}$$
$$\text{B: 1 } \rightleftharpoons \text{ 2, right has more}$$
Only B has more gas moles on the right, so only B shifts right when pressure is lowered.

**Combine both conditions**

We need endothermic forward AND more gas moles on the right. That combination is met by the dissociation of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ to $\text{NO}_2$.

options.A: Forward reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H = +40$), so heating does shift it right. However, there are 2 moles of gas on each side ($\text{H}_2 + \text{CO}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}$), so changing pressure has no effect. It fails the pressure condition.
options.B: Forward reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H = +58 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$), so increasing temperature shifts equilibrium right to absorb heat. There is 1 mole of gas on the left and 2 moles on the right ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_4 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2$), so decreasing pressure shifts equilibrium right toward more moles. Both conditions are met.
options.C: Forward reaction is strongly exothermic ($\Delta H = -197$), so increasing temperature shifts equilibrium left, not right. Also 3 moles of gas go to 2 moles, so decreasing pressure shifts it left toward more moles. It is the opposite of what is wanted.
options.D: Forward reaction is exothermic ($\Delta H = -10$), so increasing temperature shifts equilibrium left. Although gas moles are equal (2 on each side) so pressure has no effect, it already fails the temperature condition. A common trap is to confuse the sign of $\Delta H$.
